summary: This document presents requirements for MPLS-TP Shared Mesh Protection not based on control-plane support. It expands on RFC 5654 and RFC 6372.

eli5.summary: Backup paths can be shared among many routes to save resources. This RFC lists what is needed for such sharing.

questions: soft vs hard preemption in smp
mpls-tp protection without a control plane
subtitle: What any data-plane mechanism must do so several MPLS-TP backup paths can safely share the same resources.

tldr.problem: Dedicating a full backup path to every working path wastes resources, and 1:n or m:n protection only works when all paths have the same endpoints. Some operators also coordinate protection switching in the data plane, not a control plane.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists network objectives for Shared Mesh Protection (SMP): pre-configured working and protection paths, shared segments identified in advance, priority-based preemption, notification, reversion, timers and a communication channel.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a protocol: it defines no messages or logic, and leaves those to solutions that must meet the objectives.

sections.title: Why Share Protection Resources
sections.content:
The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) can protect traffic by switching it to a pre-established backup path. With 1+1 protection, resources are allocated for both the working and protection paths. With 1:1 protection, the same resources are allocated but the protection path can carry preemptible extra traffic.

1:n and m:n protection let several working paths share protection resources, but only if all the paths have the same endpoints. Shared Mesh Protection (SMP) removes that limit. This RFC gives requirements for any mechanism that implements SMP for MPLS-TP data paths in networks that delegate protection switch coordination to the data plane. It expands on RFC 5654 and RFC 6372.
sections.eli5: Instead of every family buying its own spare tire, the street shares a few. That costs less, as long as the cars that need one are not all broken at the same time.

sections.title: The SMP Reference Model
sections.content:
SMP protects multiple working paths that need not have common endpoints and do not share common points of failure. In the RFC's first example, working paths ABCDE and VWXYZ are each protected by 1:1 linear protection, with protection paths APQRE and VPQRZ. Both protection paths cross segment PQR and share its protection resources.

The RFC defines an SMP Protection Group as the set of different protection paths that share a common segment. Because the shared resources are oversubscribed, they are allocated but not used until a protection switch asks for them. A preemption mechanism is needed to apply business priority when several failures happen at once.

The RFC says its ideas could also be applied to MPLS networks outside the Transport Profile.
sections.eli5: Two roads have their own detours, but both detours run along one shared stretch of road. That shared stretch is where the two families must take turns.

sections.title: Control Plane or Data Plane
sections.content:
RFC 6372 and RFC 4428 observe that full SMP control, including configuration and switching coordination, is potentially very complex, so it is suggested that a dynamic GMPLS control plane handle it. The RFC notes that GMPLS implementations of SMP exist.

Some operators, particularly in the transport sector, run MPLS-TP without a control plane or have delegated resilience to the data plane. For them, all coordination of selectors and endpoints must be possible through data-plane operations. A data-plane solution is also needed where restoration must be faster than control-plane mechanisms can achieve. Protocol logic and specific messaging are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Some towns have a traffic control office that plans everything. Others want the road signs themselves to handle it quickly, with no office involved.

sections.title: Preemption and Coordination Objectives
sections.content:
SMP relies on pre-configuration of working and protection paths, by a control protocol or static management configuration. Even then, a control protocol SHALL NOT be the primary mechanism for detecting failures or coordinating the switchover. The protection relationship SHOULD be configured and shared segments MUST be identified before use.

On a trigger, the network MUST both switch traffic to the protection path and coordinate use of the shared resources, at the same time or as close as possible. The RFC describes two behaviours when a segment is oversubscribed: soft preemption (lower-priority traffic is degraded; all protection paths MAY share the resources) and hard preemption (lower-priority traffic is completely blocked).

For hard preemption: priorities MAY be assigned, and equal priority is assumed if none is. Resources go to the highest priority requester. Equal priorities are served first come first served, with tie-breaking rules defined in the SMP domain. A higher-priority path takes resources from a lower one. Once a path holds resources, it SHALL NOT be interrupted by equal or lower priority traffic. An endpoint with more than one potential action MUST verify the resources are available.
sections.eli5: If two families need the shared spare at once, the one with the more important trip gets it. If the trips matter equally, whoever asked first gets it, and the other is told to wait.

sections.title: Notification, Reversion, Timing and Timers
sections.content:
If shared resources are unavailable, the endpoints of the requesting working path SHALL be notified that switchover failed. If a path is preempted, the endpoints of the affected working path SHALL be notified too.

When the fault clears, traffic can revert to the working path or stay on the protection path. Both automatic and manual revertive behaviours MUST be supported for hard preemption, and the protocol MUST support non-revertive configurations. Normally the network should revert so the protection resources are freed for other paths.

Protection switching time is the interval from identifying a trigger until traffic begins on the protection path. Support for a protection switching time of 50 ms depends on the initial switchover, but preemption time SHOULD also be considered. SMP SHOULD use a hold-off timer so lower layers can finish their own switching first, and a Wait-To-Restore timer during reversion so an unstable path does not cause repeated switching. SMP SHOULD provide a communication channel along the protection path between its endpoints, and bidirectional switching SHOULD be supported.
sections.eli5: When the main road is fixed, you can go back to it so the detour is free for others. A short wait before switching back stops you from bouncing between roads if the repair is shaky.

sections.title: Manageability and Security
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no new manageability requirements beyond those in RFC 5951 and the ITU-T specification it cites.

For security, any proposed solution should consider exhaustion of resources through preemption, especially by a malicious actor. It should also guard against an attacker creating an alternate path to force traffic from a sensor or device onto it, which would enable pervasive monitoring.
sections.eli5: Someone could abuse the sharing rules to grab the spare for themselves, or trick traffic onto a detour where they can watch it. Any real design has to guard against that.
